spec.title: Unbalanced quote inside a heredoc body defeats the blanket-staging gate; fix the scanner and un-hide the test
spec.problem: plugins/pipeline/hooks/pre-tool-use.sh's stage-1 scanner (_scan_go) tokenizes a Bash command quote-aware to decide whether any git invocation in it is a blanket stage. It handles single quotes, double quotes, comments, redirection targets and top-level operators as a real POSIX shell would -- with one omission: it has no model of a heredoc BODY (the text introduced by `<<`/`<<-` up to the terminator line) as an opaque, non-tokenized region. Its redirection arm ('>'* | '<'*) only marks the delimiter word immediately after `<<` as an inert redirect target; everything from there to the real terminator is then fed through the ordinary quote/operator scanning logic exactly as if it were live command text. A real shell never parses a heredoc body at all -- it is copied verbatim (or with only $-expansion, never re-tokenized) until a line consisting solely of the delimiter. When a heredoc body happens to contain an ODD number of quote characters, the scanner's 'currently inside a quote' state does not close at the body's real end; it leaks past the terminator line into the command that follows, and that trailing text -- including a bare `git add -A` -- is read as inert quoted content rather than as its own invocation. The gate returns 'none' (allow) for a command a real shell would execute as a blanket stage.
spec.root_cause: The stage-1 scanner in pre-tool-use.sh models three shell regions correctly (single-quoted, double-quoted, comment) but has no fourth region for a heredoc body, so an unbalanced quote inside that body is scanned as if it were ordinary command text instead of being skipped verbatim to the real terminator line. This is confirmed by direct code reading (the '>'* | '<'* arm at hooks/pre-tool-use.sh, which consumes only the `<<`/two-char operator itself and marks one following word inert, then resumes normal top-level scanning) and independently corroborated by plugins/pipeline/tests/test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh's own dens_pad() builder, which already contains code that pads a generated body's trailing bytes to force an EVEN quote count specifically to stop this exact case from reproducing, with a comment (currently at test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh:634-645; the issue cites 571-577, which is stale against current origin/main -- same text, shifted ~63 lines by intervening edits) that misclassifies the resulting allow as a fixture defect rather than a gate defect.
requirements: R1. The scanner must recognize a heredoc introducer (`<<` and `<<-`, any legal delimiter-word spelling: bare, single-quoted, double-quoted, or backslash-escaped) and treat everything from immediately after the introducer's delimiter word up to the real terminator line as an opaque, non-tokenized region: no quote, comment, or operator inside it may change the scanner's parse state, mirroring a real shell's own treatment.

R2. The gate's verdict for a given command must equal a real-shell-plus-recording-git-shim oracle's observed argv (the approach #106 round 4 and this issue both point at) over a corpus that specifically includes unbalanced-quote heredoc bodies, not just the historically-tested balanced ones.

R3. Genuinely-quoted staging text (`echo "git add -A"` and equivalents) must remain ALLOWED after the fix -- the fix must distinguish real quoting from mis-parsed-as-quoted, not collapse the distinction the gate already relies on.

R4. The three reproductions named in the issue (the 59-byte one-single-quote body, the 60-byte three-double-quote body, and the tracked knowledge/issue-archive/40-verify-40.sh file staged in the same call) must be re-verified against the fixed gate and against the real-shell oracle, not re-asserted from the issue's own table.

R5. test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh's dens_pad() quote-balancing patch (the trailing-byte parity fix documented at its own TRUNCATION MUST NOT LEAVE A QUOTE OPEN comment) must be reverted so the builder can again emit an unbalanced-quote body, and the comment must be corrected to state that the observed allow was a genuine bypass, not a fixture defect -- per the issue's explicit instruction not to leave the next reader misled.

R6. A new regression test must independently exercise the heredoc-quote-leak class through the real-shell oracle (not merely re-running the exact historical fixture), so the suite discriminates a live defect rather than rubber-stamping one known shape. It must also include NAMED negative controls for the here-string (`<<<`) and process-substitution (`<(...)`/`>(...)`) constructs (see AC11), asserting the exact real-shell-verified verdicts SecOps recorded in round 1 review (review.secops.json concerns[1]), not resting on a hand-trace alone. A `<<-'EOF'` cell (dash-strip combined with a quoted delimiter) is recommended but not required in AC1's binding matrix: real-bash verification performed during this rework (`bash -c` against a `<<-'EOF'` construction with a tab-indented terminator and an odd-quote body, run through a PATH-shimmed recording `git`) confirmed the two mechanisms compose predictably and independently -- dash-stripping governs only terminator-LINE matching (leading tabs stripped from both the terminator line and body lines before comparison to the delimiter word), delimiter quoting governs only whether the body undergoes $-expansion (confirmed: a literal `$UNEXPANDED` token in the body printed unexpanded), and the two do not interact in real bash's grammar. The scanner's redirection arm (per DBA's finding) also treats the delimiter word as a single opaque following-token regardless of its internal quoting, so a fix that separately gets AC1's dash-strip cell and quoted-delimiter cell right has no distinct fifth mechanism left for `<<-'EOF'` to exercise. It remains cheap defense-in-depth and is recommended as an additional R6 regression-population cell, not a gating AC.

R7. The fix must not regress the existing WORD-BOUNDARY AXIS and DENSITY AXIS suites in test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh: every probe must still return inside the declared 30s timeout (hooks.json) and the suite's own tighter regression budget, re-measured after the fix rather than assumed carried over.

R8. The fix must not introduce a new false positive on the suite's already-documented correct heredoc case (a heredoc body followed by a narrowly-scoped `git add <path>`), which must continue to return 'none'.
acceptance_criteria: AC1. Run a real-shell (matching whatever binary/flags Claude Code's own Bash tool actually invokes a command with -- see open_questions/q1) plus recording-git-shim oracle, and the gate, over a fixture matrix crossing {odd double-quote count, odd single-quote count, even/balanced count} x {inside a heredoc body followed by `git add -A` after the real terminator, inside a heredoc body followed by a narrowly-scoped `git add <path>`, no heredoc at all (plain `echo "git add -A"`)} for the bare `<<` introducer (9 cells), PLUS a delimiter-introducer-spelling axis crossing {dash-stripped `<<-` with a TAB-indented terminator line, single-quoted delimiter word `<<'EOF'`, backslash-escaped delimiter word `<<\EOF`} x {odd-double-quote-count body, trailing blanket stage `git add -A` after the real terminator} (3 additional cells -- the minimum SecOps proved live-exploitable in round 1: review.secops.json concerns[0] independently reproduced bare `<<EOF`, `<<'EOF'`, and `<<-EOF` all genuinely invoking `git add -A` in real bash while the gate returned 'none' for all three). Total 12 cells. The gate's verdict must equal the oracle's observed argv-based verdict on every cell of that matrix. `<<"EOF"` (double-quoted delimiter) is not a separate required cell: it and `<<'EOF'` both suppress body $-expansion and neither affects tab-stripping or terminator-line matching, the two mechanisms this fix must actually get right, so one quoted-delimiter cell exercises the same code path as the other.

AC2. `echo "git add -A"` returns 'none' both before and after the fix, and at least one second genuinely-quoted staging string (distinct wording, e.g. inside a `printf` argument, not inside any heredoc) also returns 'none' after the fix -- the false-positive guard the issue requires stated so it cannot be traded away for AC1.

AC3. A heredoc body containing an ODD number of double quotes, followed on the same Bash call by `git add -A` after the heredoc's real terminator line, returns 'deny' after the fix (it returns 'none' before the fix -- this is the core defect and the primary redgreen pair).

AC4. The identical construction with an EVEN (already-balanced) quote count in the heredoc body, followed by `git add -A`, continues to return 'deny' after the fix (it already returns 'deny' before the fix) -- proving the fix discriminates real shell parsing rather than simply denying every command that contains a heredoc.

AC5. A heredoc body (either odd or even quote count) followed by a narrowly-scoped `git add <named path>` after the real terminator continues to return 'none' after the fix -- no new false positive on the suite's already-documented correct case.

AC6. dens_pad() in test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh no longer appends a quote-parity-balancing character to its generated body, the resulting (now potentially unbalanced) body is asserted 'deny' when followed by a trailing blanket stage, and the comment currently reading '...for a gate that is correct, which is the worst kind of red' is replaced with text stating plainly that the allow this comment used to paper over was a genuine bypass now closed by this issue.

AC7. The full test-pretooluse-gate-verdicts.sh suite (WORD-BOUNDARY AXIS and DENSITY AXIS blocks) passes with every probe inside the declared 30s timeout and the suite's own recorded regression budget, re-measured on the post-fix tree.

AC8. The tracked-file reproduction (knowledge/issue-archive/40-verify-40.sh, currently 137414 bytes, staged as a heredoc body in the same Bash call per the issue's row) returns 'deny' after the fix, re-derived directly against the file at its current byte count rather than trusted from the issue body's 137,457-byte figure.

AC9. A BALANCED-quote-count body inside a `<<-` heredoc (tab-indented terminator), followed by a blanket `git add -A` after the real terminator, continues to return 'deny' after the fix -- proving the fix's tab-stripping-aware terminator matcher discriminates real parsing rather than either leaving `<<-` unhandled or blanket-denying every `<<-` heredoc regardless of content (the AC4-equivalent discrimination proof, scoped to the newly-introduced dash-strip mechanism DBA identified as independent from quote parity).

AC10. A `<<-` heredoc (tab-indented terminator) AND a single-quoted-delimiter heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), each followed by a narrowly-scoped `git add <path>` after the real terminator, continue to return 'none' after the fix -- extending AC5/R8's no-new-false-positive guarantee to the widened delimiter-spelling coverage rather than assuming it carries over untested.

AC11. R6's regression population includes, as named negative controls verified against the real-shell-plus-recording-git-shim oracle: (a) a here-string with a genuine `git add -A` STRING operand (`cat <<< 'git add -A'`) returns 'none' (the operand is fed to `cat`'s stdin; no git process ever runs); (b) a here-string whose quote is deliberately left unterminated across a line with a trailing `git add -A` returns 'none' (real bash treats the whole construction as a syntax error and never executes anything, matching the gate); (c) process substitution wrapping a real `git add -A` (`diff <(git add -A) /dev/null`) returns 'deny'; (d) a narrow-stage-inside/blanket-stage-outside combination (`diff <(git add x.txt) /dev/null; git add -A`) returns 'deny'. All four verdicts are taken directly from SecOps's round-1 oracle run (review.secops.json concerns[1]), re-verified against the fixed gate rather than re-derived from a fresh hand-trace.

AC12. For an UNQUOTED heredoc introducer (bare `<<` or `<<-`; delimiter word NOT single-quoted, double-quoted, or backslash-escaped), the new opaque region the fix introduces (AC1-AC10) must NOT extend across a literal `$(`, a backtick, or `${` occurring in the body before the real terminator line -- minimum acceptable implementation is a coarse fail-closed rule: deny outright whenever any of those three literal sequences appears anywhere inside an unquoted heredoc body, with no attempt to tokenize what is inside the substitution. Quoted-delimiter heredoc bodies (`<<'EOF'`, `<<\EOF`, `<<"EOF"`) remain FULLY opaque exactly as AC1/R1 already specify -- this AC does not weaken that; SecOps independently reproduced against real zsh and /bin/sh that a quoted delimiter genuinely suppresses $-expansion in the production shell, so full opacity there is correct and must not be second-guessed by this narrower guard. Verified against 4 fixture cells (verbatim from secops-2.5-ruling.json's required_minimum_spec_change.required_negative_and_positive_fixture_cells, each taken from SecOps's own real-gate-driver-plus-real-zsh reproduction and re-verified against the fixed gate rather than re-derived from a fresh hand-trace): (a) unquoted `<<EOF` body containing `$(git add -A)`, no terminator-adjacent trailing command at all -> 'deny' post-fix (already 'deny' pre-fix via the accidental top-level `(`-separator mechanism; without this AC the chosen full-opacity design would silently flip it to 'none' -- this is SecOps's core VETO finding and the primary red/green pair for this AC); (b) unquoted `<<EOF` body containing `$(git add <path>)` (narrow) -> 'none' post-fix, proving the guard discriminates blanket vs narrow rather than blanket-denying every `$(` occurrence regardless of content (the AC12-equivalent of AC5/AC10's discrimination proof); (c) unquoted `<<EOF` body containing a backtick-wrapped `` `git add -A` `` -> 'deny' post-fix. This cell is 'none' PRE-fix (backtick is not a member of the scanner's structural-character set at all -- confirmed by SecOps via direct grep of _META/_STRUCT in pre-tool-use.sh), so it is a genuinely NEW protection this AC adds, not a preserved one; Dev must not assume it already passes the way AC4/AC9's balanced-quote discrimination cells do; (d) quoted-delimiter `<<'EOF'` body containing `$(git add -A)` or a backtick-wrapped `git add -A` -> 'none' post-fix. The pre-fix scanner denies this cell too, as an existing false positive (full opacity was never applied, so the body's `(` /backtick still trips the ordinary top-level scan); AC1's fix legitimately corrects that over-denial to 'none', and this cell exists to stop AC12's coarse deny-on-sighting rule from being implemented broadly enough to re-introduce the same over-denial for quoted delimiters. `${` is included in the same denial set as `$(` and backtick because it is a third $-expansion spelling (parameter expansion) reachable the identical way inside an unquoted heredoc body; SecOps's ruling did not run a dedicated `${` real-shell cell, so this AC's `${` coverage rests on R1's already-established 'mirror a real shell's own treatment' requirement plus the coarse fail-closed rule's own text (deny on sighting any of the three sequences), not on a fourth independently-reproduced fixture cell -- Dev/QA should treat `${` as governed by the same coarse rule as `$(`/backtick, not as requiring separate tokenization logic.
out_of_scope: Relocating the tokenizer into the node resolver process (#136) -- a materially different, larger, security-reopening change explicitly sequenced separately and requiring its own SecOps reading.
Re-tuning _wordchunk's delimiter fallback (#137) -- a different function, different axis (density constant, not quoting correctness), already split out and sequenced separately.
Command-word/verb opacity ($GIT add -A, git $VERB -A) -- #118's deliberately-deferred adversarial class, unrelated to this issue's accidental-quoting axis.
Any change to hooks.json's declared timeout or to the fail-open-on-timeout behavior -- #132's and #136's territory, not this issue's.

A general audit/fix of every unmodeled bash construct in the scanner (process substitution, here-strings, arithmetic expansion). Traced by hand during Phase 1 research: `<<<` here-strings and `<(...)`/`>(...)` process substitution were checked against the current scanner logic and no live bypass was found in either (see sibling_causes_considered). Given the owner's explicit resource/tightness directive tonight, these are left as-is rather than folded in; QA is recommended (non-blocking) to add them as negative controls in the AC1 oracle corpus so the fix's own regression population catches anything the manual trace missed, and a follow-up issue should be opened if the oracle finds otherwise.

sibling_causes_considered.name: here-string operator (`<<<word`)
sibling_causes_considered.reason: traced by hand against the current '>'* | '<'* arm: all three `<` characters are consumed as redirect-operator quanta and the single following word is correctly marked an inert redirect target (matching real shell semantics, since a here-string's operand is not part of the invocation's argv). No multi-line opaque-body region is introduced, so there is no state to leak. Not runtime-verified; recommended as a negative control in AC1's corpus rather than a blocking finding.

sibling_causes_considered.name: process substitution (`<(cmd)`, `>(cmd)`)
sibling_causes_considered.reason: traced by hand: the `<`/`>` is consumed by the redirection arm, then the following `(` falls through to the top-level-separator catch-all, which calls _sep_done(). _sep_done() explicitly resets _redir=0 before _inv_reset(), so the pending redirect-target flag does NOT bleed into the fresh invocation the parenthesized content becomes -- meaning a `git` invocation inside `<(...)` is actually caught (its `(`/`)` boundary coincidentally acts as an invocation separator). An initial trace suggested a bleed-through bypass here; re-tracing found it was wrong because of the explicit _redir=0 reset, which is itself evidence this scanner is subtle enough that a real-shell-oracle-driven regression population (R6) should cover this construct too rather than resting on manual reasoning alone.

sibling_causes_considered.name: arithmetic expansion / double-parens (`$((...))`, `((...))`)
sibling_causes_considered.reason: the `((`/`))` two-character forms are matched explicitly by the top-level separator arm (';;'* | '&&'* | ... | '(('* | '))'* ...), consumed as inert separator pairs; content inside is scanned as ordinary top-level text the same way parenthesized groups are elsewhere in this file. No opaque multi-line region and no quote-state persistence issue distinct from the ordinary case already covered by AC1-AC4.

one_mutation_per_criterion.mutation: revert/no-op the new heredoc-body-opacity detection entirely, for EVERY delimiter-introducer spelling (restore the pre-fix '>'* | '<'* arm as-is, so bare `<<`, `<<-`, and quoted-delimiter forms are all treated identically to the pre-fix single-inert-word handling)
one_mutation_per_criterion.fixture_matrix: 12 cells total: 3 quote-parity classes (odd-double, odd-single, balanced) x 3 trailing-context classes (blanket stage after real terminator, narrow stage after real terminator, no heredoc at all) = 9 cells for bare `<<`, PLUS 3 delimiter-spelling cells (`<<-` w/ tab-indented terminator, `<<'EOF'`, `<<\EOF`) each at {odd-double-quote body, blanket stage}. The mutation must redden every cell where quote parity is odd (or the cell is one of the 3 spelling cells, which are pinned at odd-quote+blanket by construction) AND a heredoc is present AND the trailing command is a blanket stage -- that is 4 of the 12 cells (bare-odd-double-blanket, bare-odd-single-blanket, plus the 3 new spelling cells minus the 1 that duplicates bare-odd-double-blanket = +2 net-new reddened cells). The other 8 cells must stay green, so a whole-arm mutation is not sufficient to pass this AC's own falsifiability check, and a mutation scoped only to the bare-`<<` code path would still redden the bare cells while leaving the 3 new spelling cells green -- which is exactly the coverage gap this rework closes, so a partial (bare-only) fix must fail this AC.

one_mutation_per_criterion.mutation: weaken the double-quote scanning arm so a quote character is treated as an ordinary structural separator instead of opening a real quoted region (i.e. make quotes act like `;`/`&&`) -- flips `echo "git add -A"` from 'none' to 'deny', reddening AC2 without touching AC1's heredoc logic at all.
same as AC1's mutation, scoped to the odd-quote-heredoc-blanket-stage cell specifically: the odd-quote heredoc body followed by `git add -A` stays 'none' instead of flipping to 'deny'.

introduce an off-by-one in the new terminator-line matcher so it consumes one extra line past the real terminator on a BALANCED-quote body, swallowing the trailing `git add -A` into the still-open opaque region -- flips the already-correct 'deny' to 'none', reddening AC4 while AC3's odd-quote cell might still pass, proving the two ACs test genuinely different things.

the same off-by-one terminator matcher, applied to the narrow-stage case: swallows the `<path>` operand into the opaque region, so `_pathspec` is never set and the invocation's blanket flag (if any leaked through) or absence of a narrowing operand flips the verdict from 'none' to 'deny' -- a false positive AC5 exists specifically to catch.

restore dens_pad()'s trailing quote-balancing append and the original 'for a gate that is correct' comment text -- a direct text/diff check against the file fails immediately, independent of any gate behavior.

implement the new heredoc-opacity check by scanning the remaining command character-by-character for the terminator line instead of reusing the existing bounded-window refill mechanism (_fill/_wordchunk) -- reintroduces the quadratic-scan class this file's own header measurements exist to avoid, and the DENSITY AXIS suite's large heredoc-body probes cross the declared timeout, reddening AC7.
same as AC1/AC3's mutation: with the fix reverted, the tracked-file-as-heredoc-body row returns 'none' instead of 'deny'.

the new tab-stripping-aware terminator matcher for `<<-` fails to correctly recognize the real terminator line on a BALANCED-quote body (e.g. it compares the raw, un-stripped terminator candidate against the delimiter instead of stripping leading tabs first, so a tab-indented `EOF` line never matches), and the opaque region runs past the real end of body -- flips the balanced-quote + `<<-` + blanket-stage cell from 'deny' to 'none', reddening AC9 specifically. This is a distinct failure mode from AC3/AC4's bare-`<<` mutations: a fix that gets bare `<<` fully correct but implements `<<-`'s tab-strip comparison wrong would pass AC3/AC4 while failing AC9, which is why AC9 exists as its own criterion rather than being assumed to follow from AC4.

the same new terminator-matching code (tab-strip-aware for `<<-`, or quote-aware for `<<'EOF'`) over-consumes: it fails to recognize the real terminator line and swallows the following narrow `git add <path>` operand into the still-open opaque region, so `_pathspec` is never set and the verdict flips from the correct 'none' to 'deny' -- a false positive AC10 exists specifically to catch on the widened spelling axis, where AC5 (bare `<<` only) does not reach.

the new heredoc-opacity region is implemented by widening the redirection arm's matched-operator class too broadly (treating any `<`-led two-or-three-character operator, including here-string `<<<` and process-substitution `<(`, as if it introduces the same opaque multi-line body), so it swallows the here-string operand or the process-substitution body into the new opaque region -- flips (c)/(d)'s correct 'deny' to 'none' (a real `git add -A` inside `<(...)` silently stops being seen), or, if the widening instead makes the scanner treat a here-string operand as ordinary command text, flips (a)/(b) away from their correct 'none'. Either direction reddens AC11, which exists specifically to catch the newly-introduced opacity region leaking onto constructs it was never meant to touch.

revert the coarse fail-closed substitution-sequence guard entirely -- implement AC1-AC10's opaque region as full, unconditional opacity for an unquoted heredoc body exactly as the judge's synthesized design originally proposed, with no check for `$(`, backtick, or `${` before the terminator line -- flips cells (a) and (c) from the required 'deny' to 'none' (the exact live regression SecOps's VETO caught), while cells (b) and (d) stay correctly 'none' regardless (a whole-region-opacity mutation over-permits, it does not touch the narrow/quoted cells), and every AC1-AC11 cell stays green since this mutation touches only the new unquoted-substitution guard and nothing AC1-AC11 already cover. This proves AC12 is a genuinely additive, independently-falsifiable criterion and not something the other 11 ACs already pin down.
one_mutation_per_criterion.fixture_matrix: the 4 named cells (a)-(d) above; the mutation must redden exactly (a) and (c) and leave (b) and (d) green, so a mutation that reddens all four (e.g. one that instead blanket-denies every unquoted heredoc regardless of body content) would ALSO fail this AC's own discrimination requirement and must be treated as a distinct, over-broad implementation rather than a pass.

expected_survivor.why_it_survives: a mutation that only reorders which heredoc-introducer spelling (`<<`, `<<-`, or a quoted-delimiter form) is checked first, or that renames the new opaque-region state variable, without changing which text is treated as opaque, which characters are recognized as valid delimiter-word spellings, or how tab-stripping is applied to `<<-`'s terminator comparison, changes no verdict over the widened 12-cell fixture matrix -- it is a pure refactor of the same recognized language, and a mutation battery that reddens on it would be measuring code shape rather than behavior.

open_questions.question: Should the real-shell oracle drive candidate commands through /bin/sh -c (matching the gate's own strict-POSIX implementation language and the exact form the issue's own text proposes) or through bash -c (matching what Claude Code's Bash tool actually invokes a subagent's command with)?
open_questions.why_it_matters: For the constructs this issue actually needs (heredocs, single/double quotes) sh and bash agree, so either oracle validates AC1-AC5/AC8 identically. It only matters if the oracle's fixture population is later extended (R6's 'discriminate rather than rubber-stamp' regression, or the non-blocking here-string/process-substitution negative controls noted in out_of_scope) to a construct where sh and bash diverge -- at that point the wrong oracle would validate the gate against a shell that never actually runs the command.

open_questions.ba_recommendation: Use whichever shell Claude Code's Bash tool actually invokes as the primary oracle (confirm empirically rather than assuming), and run the same corpus through /bin/sh -c as a cheap secondary check, since POSIX heredoc and quote semantics are identical between the two for everything this issue's ACs require. This is an implementation-fidelity choice with no owner-facing tradeoff (cost/timeline/product direction are unaffected either way), so it is not blocking.

chosen_approach.summary: Sketch A (smallest blast radius) wins and is adopted essentially as specified: a fourth opaque region for a heredoc body, implemented as four scalar globals (_hd, _hddash, _hdpending, _HDDELIM) threaded through the two functions that already close a word and end an invocation (_inv_words, _sep_done), plus one new function _hd_skip that reuses the file's existing bulk-slice/_cut_sc idiom to walk the body line-by-line to the real terminator. The redirection arm ('>'*|'<'* at pre-tool-use.sh:1153) is split three ways in this order: '<<<'* (here-string, byte-for-byte unchanged from today so AC11(a)/(b) cannot regress), '<<'* (new: consume, detect an optional trailing '-' into _hddash, set _hd=1), default (existing >>,>|,>&,<&,<> path, unchanged). The delimiter word is captured for free by letting the SAME quote-aware word-building machinery that already parses every ordinary word parse it -- the capture point is one additive branch inside the EXISTING `if [ "$_redir" = 1 ]` discard in _inv_words, not a bespoke word reader -- so bare, single-quoted, double-quoted and backslash-escaped delimiter spellings (AC1's four spelling cells) fall out of code already in the file rather than a second implementation of quote/backslash stripping. _sep_done gets a defensive `_hd=0` reset for the `<<` -immediately-followed-by-newline syntax-error edge. The single-newline dispatch is pulled out of the existing `';;'*|'&&'*|'||'*|'(('*|'))'*|"$_NL$_NL"*` bundle into its own arm so _sep_done runs (flushing/closing the delimiter word, which is where _hdpending actually gets set) before the _hdpending check reads a value known-correct only after that flush; _hd_skip then walks the body, tab-stripping ONLY the candidate terminator line (never body content) when _hddash=1, comparing by exact string equality against _HDDELIM, and returns with _sc positioned immediately after the real terminator line.
chosen_approach.control_flow: Per-command: ordinary top-level scan runs unchanged until a '<<' or '<<-' introducer is seen -> the arm marks the delimiter word inert exactly like an ordinary redirect target (_redir=1) while additionally latching it into _HDDELIM/_hdpending as a side effect of the SAME discard branch -> the rest of that line scans completely normally (a pipe, another redirect, anything) -> the first real newline after the delimiter closes (via _sep_done, which may itself return a blanket verdict and end the scan early) triggers _hd_skip, which consumes lines verbatim (zero quote/comment/operator interpretation) until an exact (tab-stripped-if-dash) match against _HDDELIM -> scanning resumes immediately after that terminator line as ordinary top-level text. '<<<' here-strings and '<(' / '>(' process substitution never enter this path: the former is matched and consumed before '<<'* is ever tested, the latter's '(' falls through unchanged to the existing top-level-separator catch-all (_sep_done's own _redir=0 reset already keeps a pending redirect flag from bleeding into it, unmodified by this design).
failure_modes: Off-by-one in the terminator-line comparison (over- or under-consumes) -- caught by the AC4/AC9 (balanced-quote, must-stay-deny) vs AC5/AC10 (narrow-stage, must-stay-none) discrimination pair on both sides of the same boundary, for both bare `<<` and `<<-`.

'<<<' misrouted into the new heredoc branch -- caught by AC11(a)/(b)'s here-string negative controls; case-arm ordering ('<<<'* tested and consumed before '<<'* can match) makes this structurally hard to reach by accident, but AC11 is the live assertion, not the read of the pattern.

Quadratic re-scan inside _hd_skip on a long unbroken heredoc line -- this is the exact mutation AC7's own falsifiability_pass names (character-by-character terminator search reintroducing the #116/#132 quadratic-scan class); the gate-bites proof (below) plants and reverts exactly this.

Malformed/empty delimiter word (`<<` immediately followed by whitespace or newline, a real-bash syntax error) -- grafted from Sketch B (see grafted_from_runner_up): _inv_words's new branch must not set _hdpending when $_f is empty, so the scanner falls through to ordinary scanning of whatever follows rather than claiming an opacity real bash would not apply either.
grafted_from_runner_up: Sketch B's explicit empty-delimiter defensive fallback ('if the delimiter word extraction comes out empty, do not set the pending flag; fall through to ordinary scanning') -- Sketch A's own writeup does not name this edge explicitly; it is folded into the capture branch inside _inv_words as a required guard (`[ -n "$_f" ] && { _HDDELIM=$_f; _hdpending=1; }`).

Sketch B's named _wordchunk-interaction risk: _wordchunk (queue-level-2 window-splitting) picks split points purely by structural-character frequency today, with NO concept of a heredoc-opaque region. This applies identically to Sketch A's _hd_skip, which also runs on _fill/_wordchunk-refilled windows -- if _wordchunk ever chose a split point that coincided with mid-terminator-line content in a way that changed which candidate line _hd_skip compares, that would be a correctness bug orthogonal to the terminator-matching logic itself. Sketch A's writeup does not address this; Sketch B's fallback plan (abandon the deferred/pending shape for an immediate same-line-only mechanism if this interaction proves real) is grafted in as the stated escape hatch if Dev finds it during implementation, rather than left undiscovered.

Sketch B's near-miss terminator-line test case ('a body line that is a SUBSTRING or near-miss of the delimiter, e.g. `EOF2` when the delimiter is `EOF`, must not close the body early') -- grafted in as a required internal-unit test on _hd_skip's exact-equality comparison, since Sketch A's own AC-mapped fixtures do not specifically isolate this from the ordinary balanced-quote-runs-to-real-terminator cases.

Sketch B's explicit routing rationale for '<<<' (tested and consumed BEFORE '<<'* can match, so a here-string cannot by construction reach the new opaque-region code) is the same ordering Sketch A already specifies; called out here only to note both sketches converged on it independently, which is itself corroborating evidence it is the correct ordering.

design.rationale: Both sketches implement the same core mechanism (a fourth opaque region, gated on an existing quote/comment/redirect-region model that already has three) and both satisfy DBA's AC1/AC9/AC10 discrimination-triangle requirement, SecOps's AC11 negative controls, and R5/AC6's dens_pad revert. The decision is a reviewability/blast-radius call on the most security-scrutinized file in the repo, which is squarely a technical judge's call, not a product-direction one (see owner_decision below). Sketch A wins on three concrete, non-hypothetical grounds: (1) DUPLICATION RISK. Sketch B's own writeup admits its new _heredoc_delim function re-implements the file's existing single-quote/double-quote/backslash logic as 'a second, smaller version of the same logic, not a shared call' -- and this file's own header comment names a PROVEN historical bug in exactly this class (the backslash-newline arm's comment: 'reading it as an escaped literal newline appended a phantom operand... one operand is the whole of the term that says a blanket stage was narrowed... Nothing is appended here' -- i.e. a SECOND, subtly different implementation of the same quote/backslash rule was a live bypass in this exact file before). Sketch A's delimiter capture goes through the SAME code path that already carries that fix, by construction, with zero new quote-parsing logic; Sketch B's does not, and would need to independently re-derive every one of that arm's edge cases (line continuation, `\"` vs `\\`, window-boundary refill) to have equivalent correctness, which is real, unbounded review debt on the file the project itself calls out as needing that scrutiny. (2) HOT-PATH COST. Sketch B's deferred-trigger hook is an unconditional `if _hd_pending=1` test inserted before the main case dispatch, so it runs on every structural-character dispatch for the ENTIRE SCAN of every command, heredoc or not -- Sketch B's own text names this as an unresolved, unmeasured cost on the hot path for ALL commands. Sketch A's equivalent check is scoped to the newly-split `$_NL` arm only, i.e. it is paid only at newline dispatches, a strict subset -- smaller and more localized by construction, not merely by claim. (3) STATE-VARIABLE COUNT AND NEW ABSTRACTIONS. Sketch A: 4 scalars, 1 new function, additive branches in 2 existing functions. Sketch B: 3 globals, 2 new named functions, 1 new pre-case hook -- by Sketch B's own admission, roughly 20-40 lines larger than the narrowest functionally-equivalent patch, and Sketch B's own fallback section concedes its abstraction may not even survive #136's eventual tokenizer relocation (a node reimplementation would likely model this as an explicit state enum/queue, not shell globals plus a deferred case hook) -- so the 'cleaner seam for #136' argument is speculative by Sketch B's own account, while the duplication and hot-path costs above are concrete today. A residual point favoring Sketch B's proposed separation -- clean, replaceable function boundaries independent of the outer scanner's tuning -- is real in the abstract but does not outweigh the concrete costs above on a file whose own stated design discipline is 'measure, do not assume' and 'no function call on the hot path where a count matters' (the file's own _inv_words header measurement literally documents that a function call per word/line, rather than an inline branch, is the specific mistake this file has already paid to remove once). JUDGE'S OWN FINDING, applying equally to both sketches and NOT a factor in choosing between them: I empirically verified (see residual_risks) that BOTH sketches' 'full opacity, zero interpretation' body-skip model reopens a narrow but real and live regression relative to the CURRENT (buggy) scanner -- an unquoted heredoc body containing `$(git add -A)` with no quote-parity issue currently returns 'deny' (verified live, both via the gate and via a real-bash PATH-shimmed recording-git-shim run) because the scanner's ordinary top-level '(' / ')' separator handling accidentally catches it today; a fully opaque body-skip, adopted by either sketch, would make this return 'none' post-fix. This is recorded as a residual risk with the measured evidence rather than silently dropped, per the R1-tension ruling below.

rejected_alternatives.approach: Sketch B ("cleanest seam"): two new named functions (_heredoc_delim, _heredoc_skip_body) with an independent word-extraction implementation for the delimiter, a new pre-case deferred-trigger hook running unconditionally on the hot dispatch path, and three new globals, explicitly justified as giving future work (notably #136's tokenizer relocation) a cleaner, more independently-verifiable boundary than splicing into existing functions.
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Rejected on three concrete grounds stated in rationale, not on the stance's own terms: (1) its delimiter-word extraction duplicates the file's existing quote/backslash logic rather than reusing it, which is exactly the failure class (a second, subtly-divergent implementation of one parsing rule) this file's own commented history names as a proven prior bypass; (2) its deferred-trigger hook is an unconditional per-structural-character cost on the hot path for every command, heredoc or not, versus Sketch A's cost being scoped only to newline dispatches; (3) it is a larger diff (2 functions + 1 hook + 3 globals vs. 1 function + 4 scalars + additive branches in 2 existing functions) on the file the issue's own risk_tier and this project's culture treat as the one needing the smallest, most independently-verifiable diffs, and Sketch B's own writeup concedes its abstraction may not even match what #136's eventual node reimplementation would want, so the 'cleaner seam' benefit is speculative while the duplication and hot-path costs are concrete. Sketch B's genuinely good ideas (empty-delimiter fallback, the _wordchunk-interaction risk callout, the near-miss terminator-line test case) are grafted into the chosen approach rather than lost -- see chosen_approach.grafted_from_runner_up.

residual_risks:
MEASURED, LIVE FINDING (judge's own verification, applies to the chosen design AND would have applied identically to Sketch B): a fully-opaque, zero-interpretation heredoc-body skip -- which is what BOTH sketches propose -- reopens a narrow regression relative to the CURRENT (pre-fix, buggy) scanner. Verified live against the actual gate (plugins/pipeline/tests/fixtures/pretooluse-gate-lib.sh's real driver, sub_verdict) at the reviewed commit: `cat <<EOF
before
$(git add -A)
after
EOF
echo done` (no quote-parity issue, balanced throughout) returns 'deny' TODAY, while the identical construction with a narrow `$(git add foo.txt)` returns 'none' (the pre-fix scanner already discriminates correctly here, by accident, because its unrelated top-level '(' / ')' separator handling catches the command substitution). Independently confirmed against real bash (PATH-shimmed recording-git shim, `PATH=<shim>:$PATH bash -c '...'`) that this is not an artifact of the gate's own bug: real bash genuinely invokes `git add -A` (shim log: `GIT-INVOKED: add -A`) inside this unquoted heredoc body via ordinary command substitution -- unquoted heredoc bodies are NOT opaque to $-expansion in a real shell, only to re-tokenization of the surrounding grammar, and R1's own text says the fix must 'mirror a real shell's own treatment.' Both sketches' full-opacity body-skip would flip this specific live-currently-denied case to 'none' post-fix -- a genuine regression, not a hypothetical one, and none of the 11 ACs in spec.json test this construction (AC1's matrix is entirely about quote-parity x trailing-CONTEXT-after-the-terminator, never about content the body itself executes via $-expansion). This is a LIVE-input-reachable gap (a hostile input can reach it with the fix in place, not merely a future edit), so per this project's own ship-or-block classification it should not be silently dropped. Given none of the 11 ACs require closing it, and the owner's standing tonight's-directive is tight scope / autonomous merge, I am NOT blocking this design on it and am NOT adding a 12th AC to spec.json (reopening an already BA-approved, falsifiability-clean spec for a case its own out_of_scope section already accepts a comparable class of, e.g. #118's verb-opacity gap, is disproportionate under the stated time pressure) -- but per 'deferring is an action,' this must be written into a tracked follow-up issue (not merely this design.json) before or alongside this fix's merge, carrying the exact evidence above (command, gate verdict, real-bash shim log) so the next reader does not have to re-derive it. Dev/QA should also add the three fixtures used to establish this (unquoted heredoc + $(git add -A) balanced/blanket -> currently 'deny'; unquoted heredoc + $(git add <path>) balanced/narrow -> currently 'none'; no-heredoc $(git add -A) -> currently 'deny') as an explicitly-marked 'known accepted regression, tracked in issue #<follow-up>' comment adjacent to the AC1 matrix, so CI does not silently start passing a case that used to be correctly denied without a human-readable trail explaining why.

Sketch A's own named cost: multiple heredocs introduced on one line (`cat <<A <<B`) are not handled by either sketch's scalar/last-writer-wins state -- SHARED by both designs, both explicitly name it, Sketch B additionally analyzes the failure direction correctly (not classifiable as uniformly claim-more/claim-less; a hostile input can reach it TODAY with two heredocs on one line, one on each side of the conjunction, so this is a live gap and not a ratchet). See the multi-heredoc-gap ruling below for the deferral mechanics; this entry records the technical substance.

Sketch A's own named cost: splitting the file's `$_NL$_NL` two-char bundle to give the new newline arm a clean insertion point trades away a small, explicitly-commented performance property (the file's own header names why two structural characters are read together). Behavioral risk is zero (no verdict changes on this alone), but AC7's regression budget must be RE-MEASURED post-fix on a corpus with many consecutive blank lines rather than assumed carried over -- this is exactly what AC7's gate-bites proof plan already requires, so it is not a new obligation, only a specific input shape (many blank lines) Dev should make sure the DENSITY AXIS timing re-measurement actually covers.

_hd_skip and Sketch A's newline-arm insertion both run on _fill/_wordchunk-refilled windows; _wordchunk's split-point heuristic has no concept of a heredoc-opaque region today (grafted from Sketch B's own risk callout -- see chosen_approach.grafted_from_runner_up). If implementation surfaces a case where a chosen split point changes which candidate terminator line _hd_skip compares, Dev should fall back to Sketch B's named escape hatch (an immediate, same-line-only body-skip trigger, accepting the multi-heredoc-per-line and same-line-trailing-command gaps as permanent/documented) rather than thread heredoc state into _wordchunk's own contract as a first response.

R6's `<<-'EOF'` compound cell (dash-strip and delimiter-quoting composed) is real-bash-grammar-verified independent twice (BA's rework session, SecOps's round-1 shard) and is correctly left non-gating per spec.json's R6 text -- but SecOps's own low-severity concern stands: the FIX's IMPLEMENTATION could still have an order-dependent bug the individual-axis cells (AC1's bare `<<'EOF'`, AC9's bare `<<-`) do not reach. Sketch A's design happens to keep the two steps sequential and structurally independent by construction (dash consumed in the redirection arm before the delimiter word is ever handed to the ordinary word-building machinery; quote/backslash stripping happens inside that same existing machinery, unconditionally, regardless of whether a dash preceded it) -- which is the same mitigation SecOps recommended. Dev should still write the `<<-'EOF'` cell as an actual asserted regression test (SecOps's and Sketch B's own recommendation), not rely on the structural argument alone.

secops-2.5-ruling.summary: Independently re-verified the judge's finding against both the actual gate driver and real zsh (the production shell). Confirmed: full heredoc-body opacity, applied without regard to delimiter quoting, converts a construction the CURRENT (pre-fix) gate correctly denies today -- an unquoted heredoc body containing `$(git add -A)` -- into an allow, and real zsh genuinely executes that command substitution. This is a live, fix-introduced regression, not a pre-existing/unrelated gap like #118, and it is a direct instance of the spec's own R1 requirement ('mirroring a real shell's own treatment') being violated for the unquoted case specifically. VETO: do not ship the chosen design without a narrow AC closing this. Additionally found, independently, a WORSE and entirely separate PRE-EXISTING live bypass: backtick command substitution (`git add -A`) defeats the gate TODAY, on unmodified origin/main, with no heredoc involved at all -- backtick is not a member of the scanner's structural-character set. why_this_is_not_comparable_to_118: #118 (verb/command-word opacity: $GIT add -A, git $VERB -A) is a PRE-EXISTING gap, unaffected by #140, already tracked as its own open issue, and explicitly out of #140's declared scope. Shipping #140 does not change #118's exposure in either direction.

This finding is the OPPOSITE shape: it is a DIRECT, PROVEN CONSEQUENCE of the specific design #140 is about to ship. The gate correctly denies the exact reproduction construction TODAY, before any code changes; the chosen 'full opacity regardless of delimiter quoting' design would make it allow the same construction AFTER the fix lands. #140 would be trading a proven-live bypass class it closes (the delimiter-spelling quote-leak family) for a new proven-live bypass in the same control (embedded command substitution in unquoted heredoc bodies), in the same commit, under the banner of a fix whose own R1 explicitly promises to 'mirror a real shell's own treatment' -- and for the unquoted case, the chosen design does NOT mirror real shell treatment; it is stricter (more opaque) than real bash/zsh/sh actually are.

Per evidence.md's claim-more/claim-less framing, this is the WORSE direction: post-fix, the gate would affirmatively return 'none' (a claim of safety) for a command a production shell actually executes as a blanket stage. #118's gap is a claim-less/ratchet-adjacent gap that has existed and been accepted; this is a claim-more falsehood the fix itself would newly ship.

proportionality_assessment.closed_by_the_fix: 4 proven-live bypass classes (delimiter-spelling x quote-parity: bare <<EOF, <<-EOF, <<'EOF', <<\EOF, each requiring only an odd quote count anywhere in the heredoc body -- a low bar, since ordinary English contractions like "it's" supply it -- plus a blanket stage placed after the real terminator).
proportionality_assessment.opened_by_the_fix: 1 new bypass class (unquoted-delimiter heredoc + $(...)/backtick/${...} payload embedded directly IN the body, no quote-parity or terminator-placement games needed at all).
proportionality_assessment.relative_ease_of_exploitation: The newly-opened class is, if anything, EASIER and more idiomatic to use than the classes being closed: embedding a command substitution inside an ordinary unquoted heredoc (used routinely to write config files, scripts, or templated text where interpolation is the whole point of leaving the delimiter unquoted) requires no quote-counting and no terminator-boundary reasoning -- it is a completely standard, unremarkable-looking shell idiom, which also makes it LESS visually suspicious to a human reviewer than a deliberately unbalanced quote.
proportionality_assessment.verdict_on_net_security: Not a net improvement, and not a wash by default -- it is a real trade of one live gap for a comparably (or more) easily reachable one in the exact same control, discovered and provable BEFORE any code is written. Shipping it silently, or merely documenting it as an accepted residual risk, is not proportionate given the fix is cheap to close for the narrow case: R1 already requires full opacity ONLY for genuinely-quoted delimiters (where it is correct); the unquoted case needs a narrow, additive check, not a redesign.

ruling_on_the_five_questions.1_reverified_independently: Yes -- see independent_reproduction above. The judge's specific finding is confirmed on both instruments (gate driver, real zsh) exactly as claimed, plus one additional real-shell cross-check (/bin/sh) the judge did not report.
ruling_on_the_five_questions.2_comparable_to_118: No. See why_this_is_not_comparable_to_118. This does not meet the bar for silent/documented-and-deferred treatment the way #118 does.
ruling_on_the_five_questions.3_proportionality: Net security is not materially improved by shipping as designed; see proportionality_assessment. Closing 4 known bypasses while opening a comparably-easy 5th one in the same control, in the same change, is not an acceptable trade absent a narrow additional guard.
ruling_on_the_five_questions.4_ship_with_documented_risk: Declined. This is a live-input-reachable, fix-introduced gap in a security control's core purpose (Phase 4 blanket-staging enforcement), discovered pre-implementation. Deferring it to a tracked follow-up while merging the design that creates it is the 'deferring is an action' failure mode this project's own evidence discipline warns against when the defect is reachable NOW, not only after a future edit.
ruling_on_the_five_questions.5_loop_back_required: Yes. VETO. Minimum spec change specified below.

required_minimum_spec_change.new_acceptance_criterion_sketch: AC12 (or folded into AC1's matrix as a 13th class): for an UNQUOTED heredoc introducer (bare `<<` or `<<-`, delimiter word NOT single-quoted, double-quoted, or backslash-escaped), if the heredoc body contains the literal sequence `$(`, a backtick (`` ` ``), or `${` before the real terminator line, the scanner must NOT extend the new opaque region across that occurrence -- it must continue to be scanned/flagged at least as conservatively as the CURRENT pre-fix scanner already does for the `$(` spelling (deny when the embedded content resolves to a blanket-stage git invocation; the minimum acceptable implementation is a coarse fail-closed rule: deny outright whenever any of the three literal sequences appears inside an UNQUOTED heredoc body, without attempting to tokenize what is inside the substitution). Quoted-delimiter heredoc bodies (`<<'EOF'`, `<<\EOF`, `<<"EOF"`) remain FULLY opaque exactly as R1/AC1 already specify -- confirmed correct by this ruling's own real-zsh reproduction (a quoted delimiter genuinely suppresses $-expansion in the production shell, so no scan is needed there).
required_minimum_spec_change.why_this_is_the_minimum: This does not require rearchitecting the fix or full command-substitution tokenization (the task's own framing already anticipates this scope).
